intended_object: A point of the period domain D attached to a lattice V_ℤ (a finitely generated free ℤ-module), a fixed integral bilinear form Q, and prescribed Hodge numbers {h^{p,q}} of weight n. Such a point is a Hodge filtration F^• on V_ℂ that gives a weight-n Hodge structure with those Hodge numbers and is polarized by Q (Griffiths, Periods II §1; Carlson–Müller-Stach–Peters §4). This comes from the docstring and the module documentation.
explanation:
The structure has four fields:
- `hs : HodgeStructure hℂ n`: a decreasing, exhaustive filtration on the complexification that is n-opposed to its conjugate, i.e. a pure Hodge structure of weight n.
- `htype_weight`: the weight of the prescribed type is n.
- `pol : IsPolarization hℂ hs Qint`: the fixed form is (−1)^n-symmetric and nondegenerate, satisfies the first Hodge–Riemann relation Q(F^p, F^{n+1−p}) = 0, and satisfies the second, i^{p−q} Q(x, x̄) > 0 on nonzero elements of H^{p,q}.
- `hodge_numbers`: dim_ℂ H^{p,n−p} = h^{p,n−p} for every p.

This is exactly Griffiths' description of D as the set of Hodge filtrations with fixed Hodge numbers that are polarized by the fixed form Q. Only the filtration varies; the form is a parameter. The sign conventions for the polarization are standard (Voisin / Peters–Steenbrink), and the file documents them.

The lattice is a finitely generated free ℤ-module, so V_ℂ is finite-dimensional and the Hodge numbers really are the dimensions. The weight n is redundant with `htype.weight`, but the two are tied together by `htype_weight`, so nothing changes mathematically.

The setting (an integral lattice with an integral form) is the standard one for period domains, so the definition is not too narrow. I found no Hodge-structure or period-domain notions in Mathlib.
